title: Distributed Ray Tracer
author: juliusgeo
summary: Hey HN, I'm Julius, I'm a backend engineer at Hatchet and created this demo to show off some of Hatchet's new features, primarily durable streams and serverless endpoints. Those, however, are just background details that made this significantly easier to scale. By distributing the rendering across many different nodes, orchestrated using Hatchet, it makes it possible to render quite high fidelity scenes fairly quickly. All of this would be possible on a single machine, but would be much slower without dedicated hardware (RT cores, etc). The renderer itself is using well-known ray tracing techniques, with no special considerations there. The renderer is a slightly modified version of https://github.com/ekzhang/rpt , with additional support for SDF scripting using https://docs.rs/fidget/latest/fidget/ . SDFs have been popular in the demoscene community, though perhaps not super well known outside of that, and are capable of creating some fantastic looking scenes: https://www.shadertoy.com/view/ld3Gz2 . The coolest part here is using a DSL to represent the SDFs in a rendering pipeline, and using LLMs with a chat interface to create them. title: Your Python app can run on Linux while MetaTrader runs elsewhere
author: Timur Khamatov
summary: I work on MetaRPC. One source of confusion in a Python trading integration is the word “remote.” Moving Python to Linux does not magically make the MetaTrader terminal a Linux application. There are two processes to think about: your application and the terminal it communicates with. With a local integration, you maintain a compatible terminal installation and its Python environment. With a hosted API, your application sends network requests to a managed terminal. That terminal still exists, and the broker still decides whether an order is accepted. The useful first test is a read, not a trade. Put the API key and demo-account credentials in environment variables, connect, read the account summary, then disconnect in finally . That checks authentication, broker connectivity and cleanup without introducing an open position. The new PyMT5 read-only example follows that lifecycle. Its README lists the required environment variables and installation steps. It uses the Python gRPC SDK; do not copy REST header names into a different transport and assume they mean the same thing. REST requests use the APIKey header, while the SDK handles its authentication metadata. After a read succeeds, test one small demo order. Record the returned ticket, inspect the actual position, close it and verify that it is closed. If an order request times out, read orders and history before sending it again. A timeout leaves the outcome uncertain; it does not prove that the broker rejected the order. Cost also belongs in the test plan. Hosted connections are paid while in use. Disconnect when finished, verify the terminal state in the portal, and estimate usage from the schedule you actually expect to run. The SDK's cleanup attempt is not proof that a failed network request reached the server. There is no universal winner between local and hosted integration. Choose based on who will maintain the terminal, where your application must run, which operations you need and how you will recover from failure. Deployment comparison · Python walkthrough

title: Can You Use a Real-Time Forex API for Free? A Trial Has Limits
author: wang vball
summary: A free forex API can be useful for evaluating live quotes, but “free” does not necessarily mean ongoing access for a production application. Check the trial expiry, permitted currency pairs, request and subscription budgets, historical access, and usage rights separately. TickDB provides a concrete example: its documented Free plan is a seven-day trial, not an unlimited free production tier. The useful question is not just whether an API returns EURUSD. It is whether the access you can test today covers the application you intend to operate next month. A prototype that retrieves one quote can succeed even when a multi-user dashboard would exceed a connection limit, need an unavailable pair, or require historical queries outside the plan. This article uses TickDB's public documentation, checked on November 13, 2026, to show how to make that decision. It is not a provider ranking or a live performance benchmark. The same evaluation questions can be applied to another supplier, but the numerical limits below belong to TickDB. A free trial is a time-limited evaluation TickDB's Pricing documentation lists a seven-day Free trial with selected symbols, five concurrent subscriptions, one WebSocket connection, and an API rate limit of 30 requests per minute. It includes real-time quotes and real-time candlesticks. Those are separate constraints: access to the quote endpoint does not establish that every currency pair is included, and one open connection does not imply unlimited subscriptions. Start by writing down the exact pairs and data your prototype needs. A currency converter using occasional snapshots has a different workload from a streaming dashboard. Test those specific symbols with the actual evaluation account rather than assuming that a supported-market list is the same as an account's entitlement list. For a permanent free tier, the evidence must explicitly establish continuing access after the trial period. The documented seven-day trial does not do that. An application intended to run indefinitely therefore needs a plan for what happens when evaluation access ends, even if its traffic is small. Separate request volume from streaming capacity REST requests, open WebSocket connections, and concurrent subscriptions measure different activity. Reducing polling can lower REST traffic without changing how many symbols remain subscribed. Combining updates on one connection can reduce the connection count without reducing the subscription count. Consider an illustrative workload, not a measured service result. Polling one batched snapshot every two seconds produces 30 requests per minute. That reaches the documented Free request limit before allowing for any other calls. Polling every three seconds produces 20 requests per minute, leaving ten requests of arithmetic headroom, but it does not prove the server will accept a burst or that other applications sharing the key are idle. A rate limit is not a recommended target operating level. The Ticker Snapshot documentation allows up to 50 symbols per request. That endpoint maximum is not a grant of access to 50 trial symbols. Batch only symbols the account can actually access, and budget all calls sharing the relevant allowance. For a streaming implementation, verify connection and subscription limits independently instead of treating “WebSocket supported” as the end of the check. Figure 1. An evaluation checklist, not a measured benchmark or a guarantee of account access. Candlestick access does not promise arbitrary history A common surprise is that a plan can expose candlesticks while restricting time-range queries. TickDB's Candlestick Data documentation says that the Free plan can query candlesticks but cannot specify a range using start_time or end_time . That distinction matters when a prototype becomes a backtest. A chart showing currently available bars is not evidence that the same account can retrieve the last year for every pair. The pricing page lists historical data separately, while the endpoint documentation describes the exact parameter restriction. Read both before deciding whether a free evaluation can answer your research question. Make the historical requirement explicit: pairs, interval, requested date range, and any completeness checks. If a query mode is unavailable, preserve that result. Removing the dates until the endpoint returns something may help diagnose the issue, but it changes the question and cannot validate the original backtest requirement. Also account for the last returned candle still forming; its changing values are not automatically a data error. Make access failures visible in the integration A failed request should tell you whether to change the workload, check permissions, or investigate transport. Repeating a forbidden request does not create permission. TickDB documents 3001 as a rate-limit error, 3006 as product access unavailable on the current plan, 3008 as unavailable candlestick time-range queries, and 3009 as an endpoint permission problem. The following Python example makes one snapshot request and records a useful failure category. It requires the third-party requests package and an API key supplied through the TICKDB_API_KEY environment variable. Run it on a trusted backend, not in a public browser bundle. It is an implementation example based on the documented contract; no live account or market-data performance was tested for this article. import os import requests def fetch_forex_snapshot ( symbol = "EURUSD" ) : response = requests . get ( "https://api.tickdb.ai/v1/market/ticker" , params = { "symbols" : symbol , "type" : "forex" } , headers = { "X-API-Key" : os . environ [ "TICKDB_API_KEY" ] } , timeout = 10 , ) try : body = response . json ( ) except ValueError as exc : raise RuntimeError ( f "HTTP {response.status_code}: non-JSON response" ) from exc if not isinstance ( body , dict ) : raise RuntimeError ( "Unexpected response shape" ) code = str ( body . get ( "code" , "UNKNOWN" ) ) if not response . ok or code != "0" : if code == "3001" : retry_after = response . headers . get ( "Retry-After" ) action = f "Rate limited; Retry-After={retry_after!r}" elif code in { "3006" , "3008" , "3009" } : action = "Check product, query-mode, or endpoint access" else : action = "Inspect the documented error before retrying" raise RuntimeError ( f "HTTP {response.status_code}, code={code}: {action}" ) rows = body . get ( "data" ) if not isinstance ( rows , list ) or not rows : raise RuntimeError ( "No usable snapshot returned" ) return rows The code checks both the HTTP outcome and the business code, normalizing the latter because error codes can be strings or integers. It deliberately performs no automatic retry. A production caller should honor the documented rate-limit wait, use bounded retries for transient failures, and stop on permission failures until the request or account changes. Connection exceptions and timeouts also need handling at that caller boundary. A successful response is still only one piece of evidence. Inspect the requested symbol, its timestamp, and the fields your application uses. The ticker documentation makes fields such as bid and ask conditional on availability; a generic response schema is not proof that every forex instrument returns them. Do not invent missing values simply to make a comparison screen complete. Figure 2. Proposed failure handling. Different failure causes require different next actions. Choose paid access from requirements rather than the largest number The public monthly pricing lists Starter at $99 per month, Professional at $299, and Enterprise at $899. Their documented API limits are 60, 600, and 1,800 requests per minute respectively, with one, three, and ten WebSocket connections. These figures describe monthly plans as checked on November 13, 2026; other billing periods and later pricing changes should be verified separately. Those numbers are useful only after you know the binding constraint. A higher request allowance may solve polling pressure but not an unsupported field or an unsuitable data license. Likewise, a larger historical allowance does not by itself establish the coverage or quality needed by a particular strategy. Ask the provider to resolve any market-specific ambiguity before treating a general pricing table as a production promise. Public display, redistribution, storage, and commercial use also require their own rights check. The technical access facts above do not establish those permissions. Obtain the terms applicable to your intended use rather than inferring them from a working key or a paid price. The decision a free evaluation should produce Finish the trial with a short acceptance record: which pairs worked, which data and date ranges were available, the workload you tested, failures observed, the expected paid configuration, and unresolved usage rights. Keep documented limits separate from measurements you actually made. A free forex API is enough for an evaluation when it lets you answer those questions within its time and access limits. It is enough for ongoing production only when the continuing plan, workload, market coverage, and rights all support that use. If one remains unverified, the honest result is an open requirement, not a claim that the integration is ready.

title: What Presidio misses for Canadian PII, and what I did about it
author: Arthur Jin
summary: I'm Arthur, a systems engineer at Geek+ in Toronto, where I work on warehouse automation integrations. This post is about canpii , an open-source package I wrote that adds Canadian identifiers to Microsoft Presidio , a widely used open-source PII detector. The problem, in one support ticket Here is a made-up ticket. Every identifier in this post is synthetic. Ticket from Jane Tremblay: the clinic rejected my health card, OHIP 1234-567-897 AB. Please also update our business number to 123456782 RT 0001. And one in French: Bonjour, mon numéro d'assurance maladie est BOUF 9451 1419 et la pharmacie le refuse. The first contains an Ontario health number (OHIP) and a CRA Business Number with a GST/HST program account. The second contains a Québec health insurance number (RAMQ). I ran both through stock Presidio 2.2.366: the default recognizers, nothing added, with the small spaCy models for English and French, and a score threshold of 0.4. This is what it found in the English ticket: PERSON 'Jane Tremblay' 0.85 PHONE_NUMBER '1234-567-897' 0.40 DATE_TIME '123456782' 0.85 US_PASSPORT '123456782' 0.40 After anonymization: Ticket from <PERSON>: the clinic rejected my health card, OHIP <PHONE_NUMBER> AB. Please also update our business number to <DATE_TIME> RT 0001. The health number is masked, but as a phone number, and its version code AB is left behind. The Business Number is masked as a date, and the program account RT 0001 is left behind. If your policy says "block health numbers" or "allow phone numbers", it does the wrong thing in both cases. In the French ticket, stock Presidio found nothing. The RAMQ number went through unchanged. Why Canadian identifiers are awkward There is no single "Canadian health number". Each province issues its own: Ontario: 10 digits plus an optional one- or two-letter version code. Québec: 4 letters and 8 digits, with the holder's birth date embedded. British Columbia: 10 digits starting with 9, with a MOD-11 check digit. Alberta: 9 digits, with no published check digit. So one entity needs several recognizers, and they differ in how much you can trust a match. A BC number that passes its checksum is strong evidence. A 9-digit Alberta number is just nine digits; only the words around it ("AHCIP", "health number") tell you what it is. Passport numbers (2 letters and 6 digits) and bank account numbers (7 to 12 digits) are in the same position: without context they look like order IDs. Then there is French. The context words that raise a score have to exist in both languages: "carte santé", "assurance maladie", "permis de conduire", "numéro d'entreprise". Context matching has its own trap. Presidio does ship a Canadian SIN recognizer (disabled by default), and one of its context words is "sin". Presidio's default matching is by substring, and "sin" is a substring of "bu* sin *ess". With that recognizer enabled: Number on file: 130-692-544. CA_SIN 0.5 Our business number is 130-692-544. CA_SIN 0.85 The word "business" raises the SIN score from 0.5 to 0.85, as much as the word "SIN" itself does. I reported this upstream as presidio#2459 . canpii's analyzer uses whole-word context matching, where the second sentence scores 0.5. What canpii does canpii adds five entities in Presidio's own style: CA_HEALTH_NUMBER (Ontario, Québec, BC, Alberta), CA_PASSPORT , CA_BN , CA_BANK_ACCOUNT and CA_DRIVER_LICENSE (Ontario, Québec, BC). Each recognizer has English and French context words, and validation where an official rule exists: the BC checksum, the RAMQ birth date, the CRA program identifiers. It also turns on Presidio's own SIN and postal code recognizers. from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine from canpii import create_analyzer , get_preset analyzer = create_analyzer ( languages = [ "en" , "fr" ] ) entities = get_preset ( "pipeda" ) . entity_list ( ) tickets = [ ( "en" , "Ticket from Jane Tremblay: the clinic rejected my health card, " "OHIP 1234-567-897 AB. Please also update our business number to 123456782 RT 0001." , ) , ( "fr" , "Bonjour, mon numéro d'assurance maladie est BOUF 9451 1419 et la pharmacie le refuse." ) , ] for language , text in tickets : results = analyzer . analyze ( text , language = language , entities = entities ) print ( AnonymizerEngine ( ) . anonymize ( text = text , analyzer_results = results ) . text ) Output: Ticket from <PERSON>: the clinic rejected my health card, OHIP <CA_HEALTH_NUMBER>. Please also update our business number to <CA_BN>. Bonjour, mon numéro d'assurance maladie est <CA_HEALTH_NUMBER> et la pharmacie le refuse. The version code and the program account are now part of the match, and the French ticket is handled. pipeda is one of three presets (with phipa and quebec_law25 ): lists of entity types that are a starting point for a policy. They are not legal advice. Numbers The repository has a benchmark: 1,740 bilingual template sentences with 700 labeled occurrences of the five identifiers above, some with a context word and some without. I ran the positives through stock Presidio and through Presidio + canpii at threshold 0.4. Recall: Entity Gold spans Stock: right entity Stock: flagged as anything canpii: right entity CA_HEALTH_NUMBER 240 0.000 0.696 0.863 CA_PASSPORT 60 0.000 0.183 0.667 CA_BN 60 0.000 0.500 0.933 CA_BANK_ACCOUNT 160 0.000 0.506 0.625 CA_DRIVER_LICENSE 180 0.000 0.483 0.778 All five 700 0.000 0.537 0.776 "Flagged as anything" is the generous reading for stock Presidio: any part of the identifier tagged as any entity, as in the ticket above. It covers the whole identifier for only 0.360 of the spans. The caveat matters more than the table. I wrote the template sentences, so this is a regression benchmark, not an estimate of accuracy on real text. Recall is also only half of it: on the same corpus canpii's precision ranges from 0.71 (bank numbers) to 1.00. The method and full tables are in benchmarks/RESULTS.md . Where it falls short No context, no match, for the weak patterns. All of canpii's misses in that table are sentences without a context word. There it found 0 of 20 passport numbers and 0 of 60 bank numbers. That is deliberate, because flagging every 7-digit number is worse, but it means free-form text will have misses. Provinces are missing. Health cards for Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Nova Scotia, and driver's licences for Alberta and Manitoba, are not covered yet. Neither are New Brunswick, PEI, Newfoundland and Labrador or the territories. The French needs a native review. The French context words and test sentences have not been reviewed by someone who writes Québec French every day. The benchmark is synthetic. A more realistic corpus is an open issue. Issues #1 to #8 cover these gaps. Each province is a self-contained recognizer, validator and tests, with a recipe in CONTRIBUTING.md. If you know your province's card format, that is a small pull request. Two rules: every format rule cites a source, and no real identifiers, ever. Links Live demo (synthetic examples): https://canpii.streamlit.app Repository: https://github.com/ArthurJZL/canpii PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/canpii/ ( pip install canpii ) Upstream context bug: https://github.com/data-privacy-stack/presidio/issues/2459

title: The Relevance of Software Engineering in Web Applications
author: Numbort Tonia
summary: Introduction Software engineering plays an important role in the development of modern web applications. Today, web applications are used in almost every area of life, including education, banking, communication, healthcare, entertainment, and online shopping. Developing a successful web application requires more than just writing code. It involves proper planning, designing, testing, security, and maintenance. These activities are part of software engineering. However, with the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI), developers can now create applications by simply describing what they want. This practice is commonly known as vibe coding. Although vibe coding makes development faster and easier, depending entirely on AI without understanding the generated code can create serious problems. This article discusses the relevance of software engineering in web applications and highlights the dangers of vibe coding and developing WebApps without proper software engineering practices. 1. Meaning of Software Engineering Software engineering is the systematic application of engineering principles, methods, and techniques to the development, testing, operation, and maintenance of software. It is not just about writing code. It involves several stages: Requirement analysis. System design. Coding and implementation. Software testing. Deployment. Maintenance. For example, when developing an online shopping application, developers must plan how customers will register, log in, search for products, make payments, and track their orders. Without proper planning, the application may contain errors and security problems. 2. Relevance of Software Engineering in Web Applications Software engineering is important in WebApps for several reasons. A. Security Web applications often store personal information such as names, passwords, addresses, and payment details. Software engineering helps developers protect this information against unauthorized access and cyberattacks. B. Reliability A good web application should perform its functions correctly. Software engineering encourages proper testing to identify and correct errors before the application is released. C. Easy Maintenance Web applications need regular updates and improvements. Properly organized code makes it easier for developers to correct errors and add new features. D. Scalability Scalability is the ability of an application to handle an increasing number of users. Proper software design helps an application grow without constantly failing. E. Cost Reduction Planning and testing help developers identify problems early. This reduces the cost of correcting errors after an application has been released. F. Better User Experience Software engineering helps developers create applications that are easy to use, responsive, accessible, and efficient. 3. Understanding Vibe Coding Vibe coding is a modern approach to software development where a person uses ordinary language to describe an application and depends on Artificial Intelligence tools to generate much of the code. For example, a person may tell an AI tool: "Create an online shopping website where customers can register, buy products, and make payments." The AI tool may generate HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other parts of the application. Vibe coding can help beginners learn programming, build prototypes, and complete simple tasks faster. However, problems arise when developers accept AI-generated code without understanding, reviewing, or testing it. 4. Demerits and Dangers of Vibe Coding Although vibe coding has advantages, it also has several disadvantages. A. Security Vulnerabilities AI-generated code may contain security weaknesses. For example, a login system may fail to protect user accounts properly or may allow unauthorized users to access restricted pages. B. Poor Code Quality AI can generate code that works but is poorly organized. It may contain repeated code, unnecessary functions, and complicated structures. C. Lack of Proper Testing Some developers assume that an application is ready simply because it opens successfully. However, the application may still contain errors that appear when users interact with it. D. Database Problems AI-generated applications may have poorly designed databases. This can cause duplicated information, incorrect relationships, and difficulties managing records. E. Overdependence on AI Developers who depend entirely on AI may fail to develop their programming and problem-solving skills. They may struggle to identify and correct errors without AI assistance. F. Privacy Risks Sharing passwords, API keys, or private customer information with unapproved AI tools can expose sensitive information. G. Difficult Maintenance When developers do not understand the code generated by AI, updating and improving the application can become difficult. H. False Confidence An application may look professional because it has attractive colours, buttons, and dashboards. However, its appearance does not guarantee that it is secure, reliable, or functional. 5. Dangers of Developing WebApps Without Software Engineering Developing web applications without following proper software engineering practices can lead to serious problems. Some of these dangers include: Data breaches: Private customer information may be exposed to unauthorized people. Financial losses: Poorly developed payment systems may cause incorrect transactions. System failure: Applications may stop working when many people access them. Data loss: Poor database management may result in missing or damaged information. Poor performance: Unorganized code may make an application slow. Unauthorized access: Weak security may allow people to access restricted accounts. High maintenance costs: Poorly structured applications are difficult to update. Loss of customer trust: Users may stop using applications that frequently fail or expose their information. These problems show that developing a WebApp is not just about making it attractive. It must also be secure, reliable, and functional. 6. How Software Engineering Can Prevent These Problems Developers can reduce these risks by following proper software engineering practices. 1. Requirement Analysis: Developers should understand what the application is expected to do before development begins. 2. System Design: Developers should plan the structure of the application, database, and relationships between different components. 3. Proper Coding: Developers should write clean, organized, reusable, and understandable code. 4. Software Testing: Applications should be tested to identify errors and confirm that their features work correctly. 5. Database Security: Developers should protect stored information through appropriate access controls and secure database practices. 6. Code Review: Code should be reviewed to identify errors and security weaknesses. 7. Regular Maintenance: Applications should receive regular updates, corrections, and security improvements. 8. Responsible Use of AI: AI should be used as an assistant rather than a replacement for programming knowledge and software engineering practices. 7. Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence and Software Engineering Artificial Intelligence is changing the way software is developed. AI tools help developers generate code, understand programming concepts, and complete tasks faster. However, AI does not remove the need for software engineering. Developers must still understand, review, test, and improve the code generated by AI. For example, AI can generate a registration form, but the developer must ensure that user information is validated, passwords are properly protected, and the database stores information correctly. The best approach is to combine AI tools with software engineering principles. Conclusion Software engineering is an essential part of developing successful web applications. It helps ensure that applications are properly planned, designed, developed, tested, secured, and maintained. Although vibe coding has made software development easier and faster, depending completely on AI-generated code without proper understanding and testing can create serious security, privacy, performance, and maintenance problems. A professional web application should not be judged only by its appearance or how quickly it was developed. Its quality should also be measured by its security, reliability, performance, and ability to meet users' needs. Therefore, developers should not abandon software engineering because of Artificial Intelligence. Instead, they should use AI alongside proper engineering practices. The future of web development should not only be about generating code quickly, but about building applications that are secure, reliable, useful, and sustainable. title: Étiquette, contraste, clavier : trois défauts fréquents des formulaires
author: Claren
summary: Une demande d’acte, une inscription, une commande : tout passe par un formulaire. Trois situations que l’on retrouve souvent, chacune reproductible sur votre propre site en une minute. 1. Le texte d’exemple qui sert d’étiquette Le test. Cliquez dans un champ et commencez à écrire. Si le nom du champ disparaît, il n’était qu’un texte d’exemple. Ce que cela change. Une personne qui revient sur le formulaire ne sait plus ce qu’elle a saisi où. Avec un lecteur d’écran, le champ peut être annoncé sans nom. La correction. Une étiquette visible, placée au-dessus du champ, et associée à lui dans le code. Le texte d’exemple peut rester, en complément. 2. Le texte gris sur fond clair Le test. Relevez les couleurs réellement utilisées pour le texte et son fond, puis mesurez leur rapport avec un outil de contraste. Un examen visuel au soleil peut révéler une gêne, mais il ne permet pas de conclure au respect du seuil. Sur un dégradé ou une image, vérifiez les zones derrière le texte. Ce que cela change. Les consignes et les erreurs sont précisément les textes qu’il faut lire pour finir. Une vision qui baisse avec l’âge suffit à les perdre. La correction. Un rapport de contraste d’au moins 4,5 pour 1 entre le texte et son fond, pour les textes de taille courante. Cela se mesure avec un outil gratuit, page par page. 3. Le bouton qu’on ne peut pas atteindre au clavier Le test. Posez la souris et avancez avec la touche Tab. Chaque élément atteint doit se voir. Si le focus disparaît, ou saute un bouton, quelqu’un ne pourra pas l’utiliser. Ce que cela change. Les personnes qui naviguent au clavier, avec un contacteur ou avec un lecteur d’écran, dépendent de cet ordre et de ce repère visible. La correction. Des éléments interactifs natifs, un ordre de tabulation qui suit la lecture, et un indicateur de focus visible qui n’est pas retiré par la feuille de style. Ce que ces trois tests ne disent pas Ils repèrent des défauts, ils ne mesurent pas la conformité. Un audit selon le RGAA examine chaque critère sur un échantillon représentatif, avec des outils d’assistance. Ces trois tests sont un bon premier pas pour savoir si le sujet mérite d’être ouvert. Sources Critères et tests du RGAA , thématiques formulaires, couleurs et navigation. À lire ensuite : À quoi ressemble une fiche de correction . title: How I Made a 400-Page Storefront Load in Under a Second
author: Shipon Talukdar All Project
summary: I run a small e-commerce storefront — an online vape shop in Dubai with about 170 products, 37 categories, and 420 URLs in the sitemap. It is built with Next.js 16, Supabase, and Cloudinary, and it runs on the Vercel free plan, which means every deployment and every CPU second counts. Here is what actually moved the needle on speed, and what did not. The problem: product pages took 4–5 seconds Before the change, a product page took 1.3–1.6 seconds just to show the product name, 2.1–2.3 seconds for the buy box, and 4–5.3 seconds total on a slow connection, at 364KB. The page was server-rendered on every visit: product data, reviews, and related products all fetched per request. On a free plan, that is both slow and expensive. What worked: pre-render everything at build time The single biggest win was generateStaticParams on the product and category pages. All 405 static pages now build in about 32 seconds, and a visit serves a pre-rendered page. Measured after the change: product name and buy box arrive with the first byte, TTFB 0.58–0.69s, total 0.79–0.91s, 246KB. Same content, same URLs — the work just moved from request time to build time. Two details mattered: The build must never fail because the database is down. The static-params function wraps the database call in try/catch and returns an empty array on failure, so a deploy still succeeds and the pages render on demand. Partial prerendering is real. The routes show as partial prerender in the build output: the static shell ships immediately and the dynamic bits stream in. That is what gets the product name into the first byte. What worked: targeted cache invalidation, not "clear everything" Pre-rendering creates a second problem: when an admin edits a price, the stale page keeps serving. The fix was per-item cache tags — every loader tags exactly what it returns ( product-<slug> , category-<slug> ), and every admin save revalidates only the tags it touched, plus the page path. Changing one product's price refreshes that product's page and the category cards showing it, and nothing else. One bug worth naming: the original code called revalidateTag after the return statement in three admin upsert functions, so it was dead code and admin edits never invalidated anything. The fix was moving the calls before the return. If your admin edits seem to "not take effect", check for code after a return before blaming the cache. What worked: reserve stock at checkout, in the database The checkout reserves stock before creating the order: a live read plus a conditional update on stock_qty (three retries per item), so two simultaneous orders cannot sell the same last unit. Over-ordering returns a 409 with a plain message. Cancelling or deleting an order restores exactly the reserved stock. When stock hits zero, the revalidation above flips the product page to "Out of Stock" on its own. What worked: reviews load in parallel, and moderation is a database flag Product reviews used to load after the product. Loading them in parallel with the product (one Promise.all ) cut a waterfall. New customer reviews are inserted with is_approved = false and only appear publicly after an admin approves them; the product's average rating is recomputed from approved reviews only. Nothing about this is clever — it is just doing the obvious thing in the right order. What did not work: chasing the homepage The homepage is the slowest page on the site (426KB of HTML, 94 images) and the only real lever is cutting content — which the shop owner will not do, because the content is the SEO. The honest answer was to leave it alone and say so, rather than burn the free-plan budget on marginal gains. Not every slow page has a fix you are allowed to ship. The checklist Pre-render product and category pages at build time; never let a database failure fail the deploy. Tag cached queries per item; revalidate only what an edit touched. Reserve stock with a conditional update at checkout; restore it on cancel. Load secondary data (reviews) in parallel, not in sequence. Keep prefetching off product cards — it burns budget for clicks that never happen. When the only fix is one you cannot ship, say so and move on. The live site is POD Shop , and the Juul range I used as the test case is at podshopdubai.com/category/juul . Same stack, same content — just faster, because the work happens at build time instead of on every visit.
