title: CR80 card size in pixels, mm and inches: a developer's cheat sheet
author: Allan Hall
summary: Sooner or later someone asks you to build a membership card preview, a gift card mockup or a "download your staff ID" feature. The first question is always the same: how big is a card, really? The answer is more precise than "about 86 by 54", and getting it slightly wrong is how you end up with artwork that gets cropped at the printer. This is the reference I wish I'd had: the numbers, the pixel maths, and copy-paste snippets. The numbers A standard plastic card (bank card, loyalty card, ID badge) is the ID-1 format from ISO/IEC 7810. The printing industry calls it CR80 . Millimetres Inches Width 85.60 mm 3.370 in Height 53.98 mm 2.125 in Corner radius ~3.18 mm 0.125 in (1/8") Thickness (typical) 0.76 mm 0.030 in (30 mil) Aspect ratio: 85.60 / 53.98 ≈ 1.586 : 1 (or 0.6306 the other way round). That's close to the golden ratio (1.618) but not equal to it, so don't reach for 1.618 as a shortcut. You'll see 3.375 in quoted for the width in some printer drivers and US templates. That's 85.725 mm, a rounded imperial figure, not the ISO value. The difference is about 0.1 mm, which doesn't matter for a screen mockup, but use 85.60 mm when you're generating print files. Bleed and safe area Printed cards are cut from larger sheets, and the cut can drift slightly. Two margins handle that: Bleed: background colour and images extend past the trim line, commonly 2–3 mm on each side, so a slightly off cut doesn't leave a white sliver. Safe area: text and logos stay at least ~3 mm inside the trim line so a slightly off cut doesn't clip them. With 3 mm bleed on every side, the artwork canvas is 91.60 × 59.98 mm (3.606 × 2.361 in). Always confirm which bleed the printer wants; 2 mm and 3 mm are both common. Pixel sizes Pixels = mm ÷ 25.4 × DPI. Rounded to whole pixels: Canvas 300 DPI 600 DPI Card only (85.60 × 53.98 mm) 1011 × 638 px 2022 × 1275 px Card + 3 mm bleed (91.60 × 59.98 mm) 1082 × 708 px 2164 × 1417 px Corner radius (3.18 mm) ~38 px ~75 px On screen, CSS treats 1 in as 96 px, so a "true size" card is about 323.5 × 204 CSS px . That's only physically accurate if the display and zoom happen to cooperate, which they usually don't (more on that below). Note the rounding: 637.56 px rounds up to 638. If you build a 1011 × 637 canvas, you've quietly changed the aspect ratio. Keep the mm values as your source of truth and derive the pixels from them. CSS: a card that scales Percentage border-radius is calculated separately against width and height, so border-radius: 3.7% gives you slightly elliptical corners on a non-square box. Drive everything from one width variable instead: .card { --w : 340px ; /* any width you like */ width : var ( --w ) ; aspect-ratio : 85.6 / 53.98 ; border-radius : calc ( var ( --w ) * 3.18 / 85.6 ) ; overflow : hidden ; background : linear-gradient ( 135deg , #12355b , #1f8a8a ) ; color : #fff ; box-shadow : 0 8px 24px rgb ( 0 0 0 / 0.2 ) ; } .card__safe { /* 3 mm safe margin, expressed relative to card width */ position : absolute ; inset : calc ( var ( --w ) * 3 / 85.6 ) ; } Make .card position: relative if you use the safe-area box for layout. For a print stylesheet you can use real units: @page { size : 85.6mm 53.98mm ; margin : 0 ; } .card--print { width : 85.6mm ; height : 53.98mm ; border-radius : 3.18mm ; } Chromium honours @page size ; check your target browser before relying on it. SVG: millimetres as user units SVG is the most honest format for this, because you can make one user unit equal 1 mm: <svg xmlns = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width = "91.6mm" height = "59.98mm" viewBox = "-3 -3 91.6 59.98" > <!-- bleed area: background runs to the outer edge --> <rect x = "-3" y = "-3" width = "91.6" height = "59.98" fill = "#12355b" /> <!-- trim line (rounded corners) --> <rect x = "0" y = "0" width = "85.6" height = "53.98" rx = "3.18" fill = "none" stroke = "#e33" stroke-width = "0.2" stroke-dasharray = "1 1" /> <!-- safe area --> <rect x = "3" y = "3" width = "79.6" height = "47.98" fill = "none" stroke = "#3c3" stroke-width = "0.2" /> </svg> The negative viewBox origin puts (0, 0) on the trim corner, so all your layout coordinates are measured from the card edge, the same way a printer measures them. Remember to strip the guide rectangles before exporting the final file. Canvas: export at print resolution For a downloadable PNG, render at 300 DPI regardless of the user's screen: const MM = 300 / 25.4 ; // px per mm at 300 DPI const W = 85.6 , H = 53.98 , BLEED = 3 ; const canvas = document . createElement ( 'canvas' ) ; canvas . width = Math . round ( ( W + BLEED * 2 ) * MM ) ; // 1082 canvas . height = Math . round ( ( H + BLEED * 2 ) * MM ) ; // 708 const ctx = canvas . getContext ( '2d' ) ; ctx . scale ( MM , MM ) ; // now draw in millimetres ctx . translate ( BLEED , BLEED ) ; // (0,0) = trim corner ctx . fillStyle = '#12355b' ; ctx . fillRect ( - BLEED , - BLEED , W + BLEED * 2 , H + BLEED * 2 ) ; ctx . fillStyle = '#fff' ; ctx . font = '4px system-ui' ; // 4 mm font size (units are mm now) ctx . fillText ( 'MEMBER NAME' , 3 , H - 6 ) ; // inside the 3 mm safe area canvas . toBlob ( b => { /* download b */ } , 'image/png' ) ; For an on-screen preview, use ctx.roundRect(0, 0, W, H, 3.18) as a clip to show the rounded corners. Don't bake the rounding into a print file, though: the corners are die-cut, and the printer wants square artwork. Common mistakes Using business card size. 3.5 × 2 in (88.9 × 50.8 mm) and the European 85 × 55 mm are paper business cards, not CR80. The aspect ratio is different, so artwork gets stretched or cropped. Rounding to 86 × 54. Fine for a quick UI sketch, but not for print files. No bleed. Backgrounds that stop exactly at the trim line give white edges. Text hugging the edge. Anything within ~3 mm of the trim is at risk. 72 DPI exports. A 324 × 204 px PNG looks fine on screen and prints soft. Export at 300 DPI minimum. Ignoring card features. Magnetic stripes, contact chips, signature panels and slot punches each cover part of the card. Keep important detail out of those zones. Trusting CSS mm on screen. 85.6mm in CSS is 323.5 px at the CSS reference of 96 px per inch, not a physical measurement. If "actual size" matters, add a calibration step (for example, ask users to hold a real card against the screen and drag a slider). Sending rounded corners or guide lines. Remove all guides before export. Checking your output If you're generating card artwork in an app, it helps to drop the exported file over a template with the trim, bleed and safe lines drawn in. A free CR80 artwork checker does exactly that in the browser (files aren't uploaded), and if you just need a quick starting design to test your pipeline with, there's a free online card designer as well. TL;DR CR80 = 85.60 × 53.98 mm = 3.370 × 2.125 in , corners ~ 3.18 mm , ratio 1.586 . 300 DPI: 1011 × 638 px (card), 1082 × 708 px (with 3 mm bleed). 600 DPI: 2022 × 1275 px (card), 2164 × 1417 px (with 3 mm bleed). Keep mm as the source of truth, keep text 3 mm inside, run backgrounds 3 mm outside.

title: I ran 42 more agent sprints on a harder task. Here's what the workflow didn't fix.
author: Huzair Saputra
summary: In the first post a Scrum workflow for coding agents looked clean: with the skill, 6 of 6 runs met every item of the Definition of Done, against 3 of 6 without it. Several of you pointed out the obvious catch. One small task, one model, three runs per side. That's a hint, not a result. So I ran a bigger one, and I wrote down the rules before I looked at a single run. What changed A harder sprint. A new Go repo with four items that depend on each other across modules. Two of them carry an authorization rule the tickets only imply. One runs a code generator that also writes into a module no role may commit. Hidden acceptance tests. Each item has tests the agents never see. This is the part I care about most, because a tidy process that ships the wrong code is still the wrong code. Seven models, two vendors. Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5 in Claude Code; gpt-6-luna , gpt-6.1-sol , gpt-5.6-sol and gpt-6-astra in Codex CLI. Each with and without the skill. Pre-registered. Hypotheses, measures, the rule for adding runs and the scoring script were frozen before the first data run. Every change after that is logged with a date. Two runs per cell first. The pre-registered rule then flagged every model as inconsistent, so every cell got a third run. 42 runs, 14 hours, all on subscriptions. What the skill still does It makes the process complete. Without it, review verdicts and the sprint reports were missing in 10 of 21 runs. With it, 2 and 1 of 21. Same pattern as last time, now across seven models instead of one. It also made runs cheaper for Sonnet, Opus, gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6-astra . I expected the opposite. And nobody, in either arm, committed the generator's write into the other module. Strong models respect write regions when you spell them out. What it doesn't do It doesn't reliably make the code more correct. Hidden tests went up for Haiku (+1.3 of 4 items), Sonnet and gpt-5.6-sol . They stayed flat for gpt-6.1-sol and Astra, and dipped slightly for Opus and Luna. The whole hidden suite passed in 3 of 21 runs without the skill and 4 of 21 with it. A workflow can make sure tests exist and get reviewed. It can't make the reviewer spot an authorization rule nobody wrote down. It doesn't help every small model. Haiku gained the most. Luna, the small Codex model, got worse with the skill. One of its runs merged nothing at all. It can get expensive. With gpt-5.6-sol , the skill's portable mode burned through tokens: one attempt alone read 17.9 million input tokens. Cost per passed hidden item went from $0.72 to $2.79. The bug in my own grader This one stung. One Definition-of-Done item checks that implementation and tests were committed separately for each item. My grader found an item's commits through its branch or an item ID in the commit message. Lanewright deletes item branches after merging, and its role commits don't repeat the ID. So the grader saw only the docs commits and failed that item in 17 of 21 runs with the skill. The separation was there. Reading the same commits from each merged pull request, with the same rules, gives 19 of 21 with the skill and 21 of 21 without. I didn't touch the frozen grader. The report shows its numbers as the main result and the re-scored ones next to them. With the fix, the skill raised the Definition-of-Done score in 6 of 7 models. Without it, in 3. You can decide which one you believe; both are in the data. Claude vs Codex, briefly Matched by list price, the Claude model met as many or more items in 7 of 8 comparisons. Codex was cheaper per passed item on the cheap and middle pairs. On the expensive pairs it flipped. Price isn't ability and the model generations differ, so I'd read this as a sketch, not a ranking. What's next Sixteen more runs start this weekend: Lanewright against the free scrum-kit in Claude Code, across four model settings, including a cheap orchestrator driving stronger roles. After that the task, hidden tests and harness go public too. Everything above, with every run's numbers, the pre-registration and the deviations log, is here: bench/hard-2026-11-10 . If you want to try it Lanewright is a paid skill on Agensi: Lanewright on Agensi . Version 1.0.1, the exact build tested here. The planning side is free. Four MIT skills take a loose brief to an SRS, a weekly sprint plan and a backlog a human signs off before any agent starts: Intake , SRS , Sprint Planner , Backlog Check . And scrum-kit stays free and MIT, with prompts in Bahasa Indonesia.

title: Extra Eyes on the Line
author: Scott Peterson
summary: On most production lines, a camera can see every part, most parts are fine, and the expensive thing is a trained inspector's attention. Inspectors don't need a replacement. They need an extra set of eyes. So I built LineSight, a demo that takes a photo or a short video clip of a manufactured part and returns three things: a PASS / REVIEW / FAIL recommendation, the visible defects with severity and location, and the most relevant entries from a library of inspection guidance. A human inspector always makes the final call. The AI's job is to focus their attention. The constraint I gave myself: the whole stack had to have zero idle cost. No always-on servers, no managed vector database burning money overnight. Everything bills per request or not at all. From finding faces to finding scratches This isn't my first time pointing code at images. Years ago I worked at HP, which owned the online photo service Snapfish at the time. I was brought onto a team building image processing technologies. We started with open source libraries like OpenCV: looking at images, running interesting conversions, and pulling individual frames out of video to examine them. Then came detection: finding a face in an image, or finding the area of interest and cropping to it. The hard part was never the code. It was the training data. To teach an algorithm what a face is, I had to break "face" down into the features that make one: eyes, eyebrows, a nose, a mouth, and where they sit relative to each other. Then I had to feed it about 100,000 sample images, some with faces and some without, so it could learn which patterns meant "face" and which were just shadows or background. Every miss meant more samples and another training run. That toolkit is all over manufacturing, for good reason. OpenCV is fast, free to run, and deterministic. It can find a part on a conveyor, confirm a label is where it belongs, measure a hole, or flag a frame that differs from a known-good reference. Where it struggles is judgment. A classical detector answers the question you tuned it for. Ask whether a mark is a scratch or a reflection, how bad it is, or what the inspector should do about it, and you're building a new model or a new pile of thresholds. Every new part, defect type, or lighting change means more tuning. That's what changed most for me. Face detection took 100,000 images. LineSight was never shown a single training image. What it knows about these parts comes from a prompt and about 20 text records in the reference library. When the bike frame came in, there was no weld detector to build or retrain. The model judged the welds on its own, and the low similarity score showed the library had nothing to back it up. A multimodal model flips that trade-off: Classical CV (OpenCV) Multimodal model (Claude on Bedrock) Best at Finding and measuring known things: faces, parts, regions, edges Judging what it sees and explaining why Training data A large labelled image set per thing you detect None; a prompt and ~20 reference records New defect type More samples, new detector or thresholds A prompt change and new reference records Output Boxes, masks, numbers Findings with severity, location, and evidence Speed Milliseconds per frame Seconds per inspection (8 to 11 here) Cost Effectively zero once deployed About a cent per image on Opus 5.5 So this isn't one replacing the other. LineSight still uses OpenCV to pull frames from video. The old toolkit does the fast, mechanical work, and the model does the part that used to need a person. The full source (CDK stack, runtime, Streamlit app, and the synthetic reference library) is on GitHub: scooteronce/linesight-quality-inspection Before you start An AWS account in us-west-2 , with model access for Anthropic Claude and Titan Text Embeddings V2 enabled in the Bedrock console. Tooling: Node.js 20+, npm, the AWS CDK, and Python 3.10+. Packaging the runtime uses Python 3.13 to build Linux ARM64 wheels for AgentCore. Cost: nothing while idle, about a cent per single-image inspection on Opus 5.5. The full breakdown is in "What it costs" below. Run the clean up at the end when you're done. Setup and deploy steps are in the repo README : precompute the reference embeddings, npx cdk deploy , then streamlit run web/app.py . The architecture Four pieces: Claude Opus 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock does the actual seeing. It receives the image frames and a prompt describing the inspection task, and returns structured findings. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 turns the model's defect description into a vector so it can be matched against a reference library of defect examples and disposition guidance. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime hosts the inspection workflow as a serverless agent. It bills per CPU/memory-second while a request runs, and nothing while idle. A local Streamlit app is the inspector's review screen: upload, inspect, see the recommendation with the supporting evidence and references. An inspection flows like this: The app resizes the upload and invokes the AgentCore runtime with base64 frames. The runtime calls Claude for structured findings. It embeds the defect summary with Titan and ranks it against the reference library by cosine similarity. Everything returns to the UI in one round trip, about 8 to 11 seconds end to end. Decision 1: Structured outputs instead of "please return JSON" The classic failure mode of LLM pipelines is parsing. The model wraps its JSON in prose, or invents an enum value, and your pipeline falls over at 2 a.m. The Claude API's structured outputs feature eliminates the whole category. You attach a JSON schema to the request, and the response is guaranteed to conform: valid JSON, correct types, enums enforced. response = claude . messages . create ( model = VISION_MODEL_ID , max_tokens = 2048 , system = "You are a cautious visual quality inspection assistant." , messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : content } ] , # image frames + prompt output_config = { "format" : { "type" : "json_schema" , "schema" : INSPECTION_SCHEMA } } , ) The schema constrains inspection_status to PASS | REVIEW | FAIL, severities to low | medium | high, and requires evidence and a location for every defect. There is no JSON parsing code in the project beyond json.loads . No regex, no "find the first brace," no retry-on-malformed loop. A related prompt-design point: the system is deliberately asymmetric. The prompt instructs the model to use FAIL only for clearly visible material defects, and REVIEW whenever the image is blurry, obstructed, or ambiguous. In quality inspection a false PASS is the expensive failure, so uncertainty routes to a human by design. Here's the prompt that does it: Inspect this manufactured part for visible surface or assembly defects. Report inspection_status, confidence, the visible defects, and a one-sentence summary. Use FAIL only for a clearly visible, material defect. Use REVIEW when the image is blurry, poorly lit, obstructed, unfamiliar, or the evidence is uncertain. Use PASS when no visible defect is apparent. Do not invent measurements or claim certainty that the image does not support. Describe each defect location in plain language; do not invent pixel coordinates or bounding boxes. The same rule applies to failures. If the model declines to analyze an image, the runtime returns REVIEW with low confidence instead of an error, so the part still lands in front of a person. Decision 2: RAG without a vector database The retrieval layer matches each finding against a library of reference records: defect examples ("deep groove with substrate exposure is high severity; hold for review") and process guidance ("reflections can resemble scratches; use diffuse lighting"). The standard recipe is OpenSearch Serverless, and that's where the zero-idle-cost constraint bites. OpenSearch Serverless bills for minimum capacity continuously, roughly $175+/month whether you query it or not. For a reference library of a few dozen records, that's absurd. Instead, embeddings are precomputed once at build time and shipped inside the runtime bundle as a JSON file. At inspection time, the runtime embeds only the model's one-sentence defect description (a Titan call costing a few millionths of a dollar) and ranks the library in-process: def _cosine_similarity ( a , b ) : dot = sum ( x * y for x , y in zip ( a , b ) ) norm = math . sqrt ( sum ( x * x for x in a ) ) * math . sqrt ( sum ( y * y for y in b ) ) return dot / norm if norm else 0.0 Pure Python, no numpy, no index, no network hop. For ~20 records of 1,024 dimensions this runs in milliseconds. It's also honest about its limits. When I fed the system a photo of a badly welded bike frame, the top reference came back at 0.338 similarity. The library has no welding records, and the low score says so instead of pretending. When a real defect library outgrows this, the upgrade path is a managed store. That's a scale decision, not a starting requirement. Decision 3: Video via frame sampling Claude doesn't ingest video directly, but it doesn't need to. The app extracts evenly spaced frames from an uploaded clip (OpenCV, sampling segment midpoints so the first and last moments are represented), resizes them, and sends them as one batch. The runtime interleaves a "Frame N:" label before each image and extends the prompt: report each distinct defect once, name the frame where it's most visible, and use agreement across frames as evidence. A mark visible from several angles is stronger evidence than something that appears in exactly one frame, which is probably glare. That last instruction matters. Multi-frame input isn't just "more pictures." It gives the model a cheap consistency check that a single photo can't provide. The schema gains a required frame field per defect, so the UI can show the inspector exactly which sampled frame to look at. Cost scales with frames sampled, not clip length: an 8-frame inspection costs roughly 8x a single image. In the review app you pick 2 to 12 frames per clip. The runtime accepts up to 20 frames and 5 MB per request, and the app lowers JPEG quality until the batch fits. Decision 4: The Anthropic SDK on Bedrock (and the IAM action nobody tells you about) The runtime calls Claude through the official Anthropic SDK's Bedrock client rather than hand-rolling boto3 request bodies. You get the Messages API surface, typed errors, and features like structured outputs with no translation layer: from anthropic import AnthropicBedrockMantle claude = AnthropicBedrockMantle ( aws_region = REGION ) Here's the gotcha that cost me a debugging session: this endpoint does not authorize against the classic bedrock:InvokeModel action. The runtime's first invocation failed with a 403 naming an action I'd never granted: not authorized to perform: bedrock-mantle:CreateInference on resource: arn:aws:bedrock-mantle:us-west-2:<account>:project/default The fix is one extra IAM statement alongside your usual Bedrock grants: new iam . PolicyStatement ( { actions : [ "bedrock-mantle:CreateInference" ] , resources : [ `arn:aws:bedrock-mantle:${region}:${account}:project/default` ] , } ) I scoped the model grants with a wildcard ( anthropic.claude-* foundation models plus the us.anthropic.claude-* cross-region inference profiles), so swapping models is an environment-variable change, not an IAM change. That matters for cost tuning. Switching VISION_MODEL_ID to Claude Haiku 5.5 makes each inspection about 40x cheaper per token (on prompts under 100K tokens, which an inspection always is). For a bounded task with a fixed schema, that's worth A/B testing against your own parts. What it costs Deploy it, use it twice a week, and the bill is two inspections. Component Cost AgentCore Runtime Consumption-based, no idle charge. A few seconds of compute per inspection, well under a cent. Claude Opus 5.5 About a cent per single-image inspection ($4/M input, $20/M output on the first-party API; Bedrock rates on the AWS pricing page). An 8-frame clip: a few cents. Titan embeddings Rounding error. Idle Zero. New AWS accounts come with free-tier credits that cover thousands of inspections. The honest caveat: this cost profile is a property of demo-scale choices. A production system reintroduces always-on baseline: a managed vector store once the reference library grows, a hosted authenticated review app instead of local Streamlit, VPC networking, image and audit-trail storage. The inspection workflow and the Bedrock calls stay identical. It's the infrastructure around them that starts the meter. Pointing it at a real line The repo inspects one upload at a time. Here's how I'd point the same pieces at a line's output. This part is a design, not something the repo does yet. Trigger with OpenCV. A camera at the end of the line runs continuously. Cheap frame differencing or a region-of-interest check detects when a part is in position, so frames are only captured when there's something to inspect. Crop before you send. Crop each frame to the part. Smaller images mean fewer tokens and less background for the model to misread. Capture a short burst. Grab several frames as the part moves or turns, and send them as one inspection. Cross-frame agreement is what separates a real scratch from glare. Route by result. PASS gets logged. REVIEW goes to an inspector's queue with the flagged frame. FAIL holds the part until a person signs off. Keep the evidence. Store the frames, the findings, and the inspector's final call. Confirmed defects become new reference records, so retrieval gets better at your parts over time. At about a cent per single-image inspection on Opus 5.5, 1,000 parts a shift is roughly $10. An 8-frame burst multiplies that by about 8. If that's too much, there are two levers: inspect a sample instead of every part, or switch to Haiku 5.5. Test both against your own parts before trusting either. Latency is the other limit. At 8 to 11 seconds per inspection, this works for sampled audits and end-of-line holds. It's too slow to gate a fast line part by part, and that's where classical CV still wins. Clean up Idle cost is zero, but delete the stack when you're finished so no IAM roles or runtimes linger in your account: npx cdk destroy That removes the AgentCore runtime and its role. No images are stored, so there's nothing else to empty. Leave the CDK bootstrap resources alone unless nothing else in the account uses them. Wrapping up Structured outputs should be your default for any LLM pipeline with a downstream consumer. Schema-guaranteed responses delete an entire class of production failure. RAG does not automatically mean vector database. Below a few thousand records, precomputed embeddings and in-process cosine similarity are simpler, faster, and free. Video is frame sampling plus prompt design. Cross-frame agreement is a real signal, so tell the model to use it. Bias uncertain cases toward human review. In inspection, the asymmetry of error costs should be designed into the prompt, not discovered in production. If you're putting vision models to work on the factory floor, I'd like to hear how you handle the human-review handoff. Drop a comment, or follow for more posts on AWS and applied AI.

title: Three Philippine Agencies Shipped AI Education Rules in One School Year. The Proof Is Still Being Assembled.
author: Yano.AI Technologies Inc.
summary: CHED's Memorandum Order No. 21 set a national framework for AI in higher education covering 2,366 institutions (Source: CHED, 2026). Within roughly one school year, DepEd launched the country's first nationwide AI program for basic education, and TESDA opened free AI courses. What has not arrived is the measurement layer that would show whether any of it changed how Filipino students actually learn. The policy layer landed first CHED's order permits AI in teaching, learning, research and institutional operations across 2,366 higher education institutions (Source: CHED, 2026). The safeguards are explicit: academic integrity, human judgment, data privacy and student welfare. Institutions keep room to apply the framework locally, on the condition that AI strengthens human thinking rather than replaces it. That condition will be the hardest to audit. "Strengthens rather than replaces" is not a metric any HEI reports, and no national baseline exists for it. A rule can be written in a semester. Proving it changed behavior takes years. Basic education got a program and a target DepEd launched AGAP.AI (Accelerating Governance and Adaptive Pedagogy through Artificial Intelligence) on January 9, 2026, described as the Philippines' first nationwide program for responsible AI integration in basic education (Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026). It targets AI literacy and ethical use training for 1.5 million students, teachers and parents. The DepEd system it operates inside covers more than 24 million students. Here is the ratio: 1.5 million people targeted for training against more than 24 million students, roughly one in sixteen. DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara named the reason: "Literacy remains one of our biggest national challenges, with many learners still not meeting expected proficiency levels" (Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026). What has actually been measured so far The clearest numbers come from ARAL, the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning program launched in September 2025 (Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026). Under it, Microsoft has begun enabling educators in 25 school districts and targets 3,000 teachers across 1,500 schools throughout 2026. Early literacy data is promising but local. Microsoft Reading Progress has assessed over 14,000 learners in 61 schools in Bais and Dumaguete, and in Cabanatuan City, 100% of learners in 3 school districts progressed to higher literacy levels (Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026). Sixty-one schools is a good start and a small sample. A national AI literacy figure needs the whole school system as the evaluation surface. The open channel: free skills, no gatekeeping TESDA partnered with UNESCO-UNEVOC and the HP Foundation to place HP LIFE courses on the TESDA Online Program, the national e-learning platform (Source: UNESCO, 2026). The catalog covers AI concepts, responsible AI use, entrepreneurship, marketing and finance. Every course is free and delivered online, so access depends on connectivity rather than enrollment paperwork. The ambition behind the channel is larger than one country. The UNESCO Global Skills Academy, which carries those courses, has committed to supporting ten million youth and adults globally in building essential skills by 2029 (Source: UNESCO, 2026). The market number is the least interesting number in this set Philippine edtech grew from USD 1.1 billion in 2025 to USD 1.3 billion in 2026, and is projected to reach USD 2.9 billion by 2034 at a compound annual growth rate of 10.87% (Source: IMARC Group, 2026). IMARC Group cites demand for digital learning platforms, career-focused tech training, investment in AI and Web3 education, and policy-driven digital tools among the drivers (Source: IMARC Group, 2026). Note the last one. Vendors are pricing the memorandum orders as demand, and when policy moves ahead of measurement, forecasts move faster than evidence. For providers the arithmetic runs in reverse. A company like Yano.AI, which builds AI-assisted learning products for Philippine schools and enterprises, does not sell against a market estimate. It sells against one classroom's adoption rate at a time, and the only honest proof is usage data from the schools themselves. What a credible measurement layer needs None of this requires new legislation, only budget lines and reporting discipline the agencies now have the mandate to create. A competency baseline across the full base of more than 24 million students, not a sample of 61 schools. Reporting from each of the 2,366 HEIs on how many courses use AI, and what happened to academic integrity cases afterward. Teacher-side instrumentation: how many of the 3,000 teachers reached through ARAL changed classroom practice, and whether it survived past the pilot window. Regional equity checks, because a national average can hide a province where nothing moved. FAQ Q: Has the Philippines actually regulated AI in schools? A: Yes, at the policy level, across three agencies. CHED's Memorandum Order No. 21 governs AI in 2,366 higher education institutions (Source: CHED, 2026). DepEd's AGAP.AI governs responsible AI integration in basic education (Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026). TESDA channels free AI and digital skills courses through its national e-learning platform (Source: UNESCO, 2026). Q: How many Filipino students are being trained in AI literacy? A: AGAP.AI targets 1.5 million students, teachers and parents in AI literacy and ethical use, against a DepEd system covering more than 24 million students (Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026). Roughly one in sixteen. Q: Is AI training in the Philippines free? A: The TESDA channel is. HP LIFE courses on the TESDA Online Program are free and delivered online, and the UNESCO Global Skills Academy behind them targets ten million youth and adults globally by 2029 (Source: UNESCO, 2026). Q: How large is the Philippine edtech market? A: It grew from USD 1.1 billion in 2025 to USD 1.3 billion in 2026, and is projected to reach USD 2.9 billion by 2034 at a 10.87% compound annual growth rate (Source: IMARC Group, 2026). Key Takeaway The Philippines shipped AI rules and programs from three agencies within one school year, across 2,366 higher education institutions, more than 24 million basic education students, and an open channel of free courses (Source: CHED, 2026; Source: DepEd and Microsoft, 2026; Source: UNESCO, 2026). The one in sixteen coverage ratio and the 61 schools of assessment data are not reasons to slow down. They are a spec for what to build next, and most of it needs no new law. So the question for every school, division and vendor is simple: if your AI contribution never appears in a national or regional dataset, can you still claim it worked? What would it take for your classrooms to be counted in the next AI literacy baseline? Sources CHED Memorandum Order No. 21, s. 2026: AI in Higher Education DepEd and Microsoft on Learning Recovery and AI Literacy UNESCO Global Skills Academy: TESDA Expands Free Digital Skills and AI Courses Philippines Edtech Market Size and Forecast (2026-2034)

title: Google’s CDN Migration Guidance: How to Protect Crawling and Indexing
author: Ali Farhat
summary: Google has published new technical SEO guidance for websites moving to a content delivery network (CDN). The central warning is that a CDN launch can temporarily increase pressure on an origin server, including pressure from Googlebot, even when the migration is intended to improve speed and scalability. The reason is a combination of faster edge infrastructure and cold caches. When a domain begins resolving to CDN edge servers, lower latency can indicate that the host can handle more crawling. At the same time, edge caches may not yet contain requested pages. Initial requests can therefore pass through the CDN to the origin, where a higher crawl rate may create unexpected load. In its official post, Moving to a CDN without overwhelming your origin (or blocking Googlebot) , Google outlines measures intended to preserve crawlability and indexing while limiting operational risk during the transition. Why a CDN move can change Googlebot activity Google describes crawl capacity, sometimes called hostload, as the amount of crawling a site can support without harming users or server performance. Googlebot adjusts its activity using signals from the site, including response times and server behavior. A CDN can make a site appear faster to crawlers because requests are answered by nearby edge locations. That is normally beneficial. But the infrastructure change can also enable Googlebot to increase its crawl speed. If the edge cache is cold, many URLs requested for the first time will still need content from the origin. This creates a migration-specific problem: the CDN may be responding quickly, while the origin is doing more work than expected. The risk is particularly relevant for large sites with many crawlable URLs, publishers with deep archives, ecommerce stores with extensive product and category inventories, and sites that already operate close to origin capacity. The guidance is not a warning against CDNs. It is a reminder that CDN configuration, cache state, crawling, and web application firewall rules need to be planned together. Pre-warm the edge cache before routing all traffic Google’s first practical recommendation is to pre-warm CDN caches before directing all traffic through the new CDN setup. The goal is for the CDN to serve the majority of requests from edge cache rather than sending them back to the origin. Cache warming can reduce the chance that a surge of Googlebot requests becomes a surge of origin requests. It also helps protect the visitor experience if real-user traffic rises at the same time as crawler activity. The specific implementation depends on the CDN and site architecture, so Google does not prescribe a universal cache-warming process. Teams should instead determine which URLs are important to cache, how cache keys and expiration rules work, and whether dynamic pages can safely be served from edge cache. For SEO, priority pages commonly include: Key landing pages, categories, and product pages. Important editorial pages and evergreen content. URLs that are frequently crawled or receive meaningful organic traffic. Essential assets needed to render pages efficiently. The important principle is not to assume a newly enabled CDN will immediately protect the origin. A CDN can only serve an edge cache hit when the requested resource is already cached and eligible to be served that way. Monitor crawl rate and origin behavior during the rollout A CDN migration should be treated as a technical change that can affect crawling behavior, not solely as a performance deployment. Google recommends explicitly monitoring and managing crawl rate during the transition. Teams should watch origin-level indicators alongside CDN metrics. A high cache-hit rate may look reassuring, but it does not fully answer whether uncached HTML requests, redirects, API calls, or other workloads are reaching the origin at a problematic rate. Useful checks during a phased rollout include response times, server errors, origin request volume, cache-hit patterns, and Googlebot activity. Search Console and server logs can help teams distinguish verified Googlebot traffic from other automated requests. If crawling becomes disruptive while caches are warming, Google says sites can temporarily return HTTP 429, meaning Too Many Requests, or HTTP 503, meaning Service Unavailable. This is an emergency measure for a short period, from a few hours to one or two days, to reduce crawl rate. It should not become a routine migration configuration. Extended or widespread error responses can interfere with crawling and indexing. The underlying issue still needs to be addressed through capacity planning, caching, or targeted access controls. Do not block verified Googlebot with blanket bot rules CDN and web application firewall (WAF) configurations often include bot-management features. These can help control abusive automation, but broad blocks can also prevent legitimate search crawlers from accessing pages. Google advises allowing verified crawlers through CDN and WAF rules rather than applying blanket bot protections. Blocking Googlebot can prevent it from recrawling existing URLs, discovering new content, or processing changed pages during a period when a site’s infrastructure is already changing. This distinction matters because user-agent strings alone are not reliable proof of crawler identity. Security teams should use their provider’s verified-bot mechanisms where appropriate and follow Google’s documented approach to verifying Googlebot when building custom rules. For unwanted automation, Google points to more targeted options, including robots.txt and rules aimed at specific bot traffic. That approach allows a site to reduce undesirable requests without accidentally cutting off crawlers needed for organic visibility. A practical rollout framework Google’s guidance supports a staged approach rather than an all-at-once DNS change with no operational safeguards. Migration stage Primary concern Supported action Before full traffic routing Cold edge caches send initial requests to the origin Pre-warm caches so more requests can be served at the edge. During rollout Faster edge latency can lead to more crawling Monitor crawl activity, origin load, response times, and errors. If origin pressure becomes severe Crawling contributes to a short-term capacity issue Temporarily use HTTP 429 or 503 for a limited window while resolving the issue. When configuring bot protection Security rules may block legitimate crawlers Allow verified crawlers and use targeted controls for unwanted bots. The framework does not replace normal migration testing. Redirect behavior, canonical URLs, robots directives, sitemaps, rendering, and monitoring remain important. However, the new guidance highlights a less obvious operational dependency: a successful CDN move requires the origin, cache layer, and crawler-access rules to work together. For agencies and in-house teams , this may also require coordination across SEO, development, infrastructure, and security. An SEO team may notice reduced crawling or index freshness, while the cause sits in a WAF rule or a cache policy implemented elsewhere. CDN changes can affect more than site speed. If you are planning infrastructure work or investigating whether technical delivery issues could limit search discovery, create a GEO Search Leads account to assess your website’s GEO readiness and identify optimization opportunities worth investigating alongside your migration plan. Frequently Asked Questions Why can Googlebot crawl more after a CDN migration? Google says faster edge latency can signal that a host can support more crawling. When a domain starts using CDN edges, Googlebot may increase crawl speed based on that improved responsiveness. Why are cold CDN caches a risk for the origin server? A cache cannot serve a resource until it has a usable cached copy. During the warm-up period, first-time requests for many URLs can pass through the CDN to the origin, increasing origin load. Can a site use HTTP 429 or 503 to slow Googlebot? Google says HTTP 429 or 503 can be used temporarily as an emergency crawl-rate reduction measure when crawl volume remains problematic during cache warm-up. The recommended window is short, ranging from a few hours to one or two days. Should a CDN or WAF block all bots during a migration? No. Google advises allowing verified crawlers through CDN and WAF rules instead of using blanket bot blocks. Targeted controls, including robots.txt or rules for unwanted bots, can reduce unwanted traffic without blocking Googlebot. Conclusion Google’s CDN migration guidance turns an easily overlooked technical interaction into a clear SEO planning requirement. Pre-warming caches, observing crawl and origin behavior, and protecting verified Googlebot access can help sites gain CDN performance benefits without creating avoidable crawling or indexing problems during the move.

title: # The Friday Deploy That Broke Checkout: A Regression Testing
author: vivek
summary: Marcus, a lead engineer at a small payments startup, still remembers the exact Slack message that ended his weekend: #alerts 18:12 Checkout conversion: 0.0% (baseline: 3.8%) #alerts 18:13 Revenue/min: $0 (baseline: $410) #support 18:15 "Your pay button does nothing??" The release that went out at 17:30 contained a "tiny" refactor to a currency formatting helper. All unit tests passed. Code review had two approvals. And yet the Pay now button silently failed for anyone using a non-USD currency. This case study walks through what went wrong, why the team's testing strategy allowed it, and how they rebuilt it. Expect code, a risk-scoring model you can copy, and a checklist at the end. Reading time: about 6 minutes. Detail Value Team size 9 engineers, 1 QA contractor Release cadence Weekly (always Friday afternoon) Regression testing Manual checklist, ~4 hours per release Automated coverage Unit tests (78%), almost no E2E The manual checklist was a Google Doc with 63 items. Under deadline pressure, the QA contractor tested the "happy path" in USD and marked the rest as "low risk." That decision is understandable. It's also exactly how a 3-line change becomes a 94-minute outage. What Actually Broke The refactor changed a helper that formats amounts for display: // BEFORE export function formatAmount ( amount : number , currency : string ) : string { return new Intl . NumberFormat ( 'en-US' , { style : 'currency' , currency } ) . format ( amount ) ; } // AFTER (the "tiny" refactor) const FORMATTERS : Record < string , Intl . NumberFormat > = { USD : new Intl . NumberFormat ( 'en-US' , { style : 'currency' , currency : 'USD' } ) , } ; export function formatAmount ( amount : number , currency : string ) : string { return FORMATTERS [ currency ] . format ( amount ) ; // TypeError for EUR, GBP, INR... } The cached formatter map only contained USD . Any other currency threw a TypeError inside a React render path, which unmounted the checkout component and left a blank page. Unit tests missed it because the test fixtures only ever used USD. Manual testing missed it for the same reason. The bug lived in the combination of currency, UI rendering, and the payment flow, which is precisely what end-to-end regression tests exist to cover. The Postmortem Insight In the blameless postmortem, the team drew a simple diagram of their safety net: Change introduced | v [Unit tests] -> checks functions in isolation -> PASSED (wrong layer) [Code review] -> checks readability and intent -> PASSED (human blind spot) [Manual regression] -> checks the happy path in USD -> PASSED (wrong data) | v [Production] -> real users in EUR, GBP, INR -> FAILED Every layer worked as designed. Every layer was blind to the same thing . The team realized they didn't have a testing-effort problem; they had a coverage-shape problem. Rebuilding the Regression Strategy Step 1: Rank flows by business risk Instead of treating all 63 checklist items equally, they scored them. Here's the model, simplified: # risk_score.py flows = [ # name, revenue_impact(1-5), usage_frequency(1-5), change_rate(1-5) ( "Checkout (multi-currency)" , 5 , 5 , 4 ) , ( "Login / SSO" , 4 , 5 , 2 ) , ( "Refund request" , 4 , 2 , 3 ) , ( "Profile settings" , 1 , 3 , 3 ) , ( "Marketing banner" , 1 , 4 , 5 ) , ] def risk ( r , u , c ) : return r * 2 + u + c # revenue impact weighted double for name , r , u , c in sorted ( flows , key = lambda f : - risk ( * f [ 1 : ] ) ) : print ( f "{risk(r, u, c):>3} {name}" ) 19 Checkout (multi-currency) 15 Login / SSO 13 Refund request 11 Marketing banner <- noisy, but low revenue impact 8 Profile settings The highest-scoring flows became the automated regression core. Everything else stayed manual or got automated later. Step 2: Add a data matrix, not just more tests The root cause was missing data variety , so they parameterized key scenarios across currencies, locales, and payment methods: Scenario Outline: Customer completes checkout Given I have a cart worth 100 in "<currency>" When I pay using "<method>" Then the order confirmation should display the amount in "<currency>" Examples: | currency | method | | USD | Visa | | EUR | Mastercard | | GBP | Apple Pay | | INR | UPI | | JPY | Visa | Five rows. That table alone would have caught the outage. Choosing How to Automate It The team had one QA contractor and no appetite for maintaining hundreds of scripted tests. They wanted tests that engineers and non-engineers could write and that wouldn't shatter on every UI change. They evaluated several options and ran a pilot with an AI-based QA platform. If you're in a similar position, you can try BotGauge on your own checkout or login flow and see how plain-English scenarios translate into executable tests without writing locator code. What mattered most to them in the pilot: Plain-language test creation , so the QA contractor could contribute directly Coverage across UI, API, and database , since checkout touches all three Self-healing behavior , so minor UI changes wouldn't create maintenance work CI integration , so regression runs happen on every merge, not once a week Changing the Release Process Technology was only half the fix. They also changed when and how they ship: # release-policy.yml (conceptual) gates : - name : unit-tests required : true - name : critical-flow-regression # the top-5 risk flows required : true blocks_merge : true - name : full-regression required : false schedule : nightly deploy_rules : - no_friday_after : "14:00" - progressive_rollout : [ 5 , 25 , 100 ] # percent of traffic - auto_rollback_if : checkout_conversion_drop_pct : 30 Three things stand out: Critical-flow regression blocks the merge. It runs in minutes, not hours. Progressive rollout limits the blast radius if something still slips through. Automated rollback triggers on a business metric, not just error rate. The Results Tracked over the following quarter (illustrative numbers from the scenario): Metric Before After Regression time per release ~4 hours manual ~12 minutes automated (critical flows) Release cadence Weekly Daily Customer-facing incidents per quarter 5 1 Mean time to detect checkout issues 40+ minutes Under 5 minutes Friday-evening pager alerts Frequent None The team didn't just ship faster. They shipped calmer . Releases stopped being events. Lessons for Your Team Passing tests only prove what you thought to test. Audit your fixtures: is your test data as diverse as your users? Rank before you automate. A risk score beats a gut feeling and beats "test everything." Test layers need different jobs. Unit tests for logic, E2E for flows that cross boundaries. Reduce blast radius, not just bug count. Progressive rollouts and automatic rollback are testing tools too. Make tests writable by more people. The fewer specialists required to add a test, the more tests get added. Quick Self-Audit Answer these honestly: When did your checkout (or core revenue flow) last get tested with a non-default currency, locale, or account type? Could a non-engineer on your team add a regression test today? If your most critical flow broke at 5:30 PM Friday, how many minutes until you'd know? If any answer made you wince, start with the risk-scoring script above. It takes 20 minutes and it's the cheapest outage insurance you'll ever buy. What's the smallest change that ever caused your biggest outage? Share it in the comments.
